parts.title: Joining a local team
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I moved to Kelham last year, I was the sort of person who watched sport on television but never played it. At school I was always chosen last for the team, and I had decided that I was simply not sporty. Then a colleague invited me to a Thursday-evening volleyball session at the sports hall. I said no three times before I finally went, mainly because she kept asking.

The first night I was terrified. Everyone seemed to know the rules, and I missed the ball almost every time. But nobody laughed. A retired teacher showed me how to hold my hands, and one of the older players told me about her first season, when she hit the ball into the ceiling. By the end of the evening, I was laughing too.

Six months later, I am still not a very good player, but I never miss a session. What I like most is not winning, because we lost most of our matches this year. It is the feeling that other people are counting on me. Last month, when I had a cold and stayed at home, three teammates sent messages asking where I was. In my old job, nobody noticed if I was away for a week.

This autumn we have entered the town tournament. I do not think we will win, but I am already planning to buy a team T-shirt, which is something I never imagined I would say.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer first go to the volleyball session?
options: She wanted to do better at sport.
questions.explanation: She says she went mainly because her colleague kept asking her, after saying no three times.

questions.prompt: How did she feel at her first session?
options: She was embarrassed because people laughed.
She felt nervous and out of place.
She was bored with the other players.
questions.explanation: She says she was terrified and everyone seemed to know the rules; nobody laughed at her.

questions.prompt: What does the writer like most about the team?
options: Learning the rules of the game.
questions.explanation: She likes the feeling that other people are counting on her, not winning, because the team lost most matches.

questions.prompt: What happened when she stayed at home with a cold?
options: The team lost an important match.
She missed a month of training.
questions.explanation: Three teammates sent messages asking where she was.

questions.prompt: How does she feel about the tournament?
options: She is happy to take part.
She is sure the team will win.
She is afraid of playing badly.
questions.explanation: She does not expect to win, but she is already planning to buy a team T-shirt, so she is looking forward to it.

parts.title: A charity bike ride
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every June, hundreds of cyclists leave Kelham at eight in the morning and ride eighty kilometres to the coast. The event started six years ago, when a teacher at the local school wanted to raise money for the children’s ward at the hospital. [1] They raised just over four hundred pounds, which bought toys and books for the ward.

The following year, the organisers put posters in shops and cafes. [2] By the third year, more than two hundred people had signed up.

Taking part is not as hard as it sounds. [3] Riders can stop at three food points on the way, where volunteers give out fruit and water, and the route follows quiet roads and cycle paths.

Of course, the weather is always a worry. [4] Last year it rained for the first twenty kilometres, but almost nobody gave up.

This year the target is ten thousand pounds, which would pay for a quiet room for families. [5] If you would like to join, you can register on the club website before the end of May.
sentences: Word spread quickly, and many people asked to join.
To reach it, they will need more riders than ever before.
Some riders wear funny costumes for the day.
There is no race, and nobody has to hurry.
Only twelve friends took part in the first ride.
The organisers have never cancelled the ride, however.

gaps.explanation: “Only twelve friends took part in the first ride” follows the start of the event, and “They raised just over four hundred pounds” then tells the result of that first ride.
After the posters, “Word spread quickly” explains why, by the third year, more than two hundred people had signed up.
“There is no race, and nobody has to hurry” explains why taking part is not as hard as it sounds; the next sentence continues with “Riders” and more details about the ride itself.
“however” contrasts with the worry about the weather: the ride is never cancelled, and the next sentence gives an example of rain.
“To reach it” refers to the ten-thousand-pound target in the sentence before, and the next sentence invites readers to join the ride.

parts.title: The town cup final
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Last Saturday I went to the final of the town cup with my brother. We arrived early to [1] good seats near the front. The weather was dry, and the crowd was [2] of excitement. For most of the game, neither team could [3] a goal. Then, five minutes before the end, our captain kicked the ball into the net and everybody [4] to their feet. We won by one goal, and the captain was [5] the cup by the mayor. On the way home, we kept talking about the goal [6] we reached our street.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You find good seats when you arrive early; you do not borrow, spend or lend seats.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: “Full of” is the fixed phrase (“full of excitement”); rich, busy and wide do not form it.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: In football, a team scores a goal; you do not win, make or play a goal.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: People who are excited jump to their feet; “pushed”, “fell” and “ran” do not fit “to their feet”.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: The mayor gave the cup to the captain, so the captain “was given” it.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: “Until we reached our street” gives the end point of the talking.

parts.title: An email about sports day
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Fergus,
Are you coming to the sports day [1] Saturday? It starts at ten o’clock, and there will be races, a football match and a tug of war. I am taking part [2] the relay race with three of my colleagues. We have been practising [3] a month, so I hope we will win. [4] you want to watch, you can park behind the school. Bring a hat, [5] it might be sunny. Afterwards, we are going to have lunch together, so please come hungry! Call me if you have [6] questions.
See you soon,
Grainne

gaps.explanation: We use “on” with a day of the week: “on Saturday”. “This Saturday” or “next Saturday” also works.
We say “take part in” a race or an event.
“For a month” gives the length of time she has been practising.
“If you want to watch” introduces a condition, followed by what he can do.
The second part gives the reason for bringing a hat: it might be sunny.
“If you have any questions” is the usual phrase after “if”.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Kelham Community Sports Club. My name is Tolga, and I’m the club secretary. I’d like to tell you how to sign up for the new season. Registration opens on the first of September and closes two weeks later. You can fill in the form online, or you can come to the office, which is next to the swimming pool. The membership fee is forty pounds for adults, and students pay half the adult price. Every member also gets a club T-shirt in their team colour. Training for all teams starts on the second Monday of the month, at seven o’clock. If you have never played in a team before, don’t worry. We have a special group for beginners, and the coach is very patient. Please bring a water bottle and wear sports shoes to the first session.

parts.title: An interview with a basketball coach
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Ulises, you coach the Kelham under-eighteen basketball team. How did you get started?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: I played as a teenager, but I was never very tall, so I wasn’t good enough to play professionally. When I stopped, a friend asked me to help with a children’s team for a few weeks. That was ten years ago, and I’m still here.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What is the most important thing in a team?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: Talking. The best teams I’ve coached weren’t always the most skilful. They were the ones who talked to each other all the time, on the court and in the changing room. If players trust each other, they pass the ball instead of trying to do everything alone.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you deal with a defeat?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: Never straight after the game. When you’re angry, you say things you don’t mean. We meet the next day, and we watch the match together and choose two or three things to improve. I always begin with something positive.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any difficult moments?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: Last year our best player broke her arm just before the final. We were all very sad, but she came to every training session anyway and gave advice from the side. In the end, we lost the final by one point, but I was proud of everyone.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you want young players to learn?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: Winning is great, but it isn’t everything. I want them to enjoy playing and to be good teammates. Many of them will never play for a living, and that’s fine. Sport can teach you to be patient, to listen and to keep trying, which is useful in any job.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Do you have any advice for someone who wants to join a team?

turns.speaker: ulises
turns.text: Don’t be shy. Go to a training session and just watch if you want. Most clubs are happy to let you try before you pay. And choose a sport you enjoy, not one that your friends play.
